newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Stability, not reform, is top priority for Ecuador.
newsitem.headline: Stability, not reform, is top priority for Ecuador.

text.p: Ecuador's protracted political crisis gives whoever emerges as the new leader little room to move ahead with badly-needed economic reforms soon, analysts said Tuesday.

"The new government's main task will be first and foremost to obtain political stability," with no time to introduce major structural reforms in months to come, said Gustavo Pinto, President of Quito Industrial Chamber.
Congress was scheduled to appoint a new interim president later on Tuesday, following the dramatic dismissal last week of populist Abdala Bucaram after only six months in power.
Before the crisis erupted, Pinto said the chamber forecast inflation this year at between 25 and 27 percent and economic growth at between three and four percent.
"Now these figures are bound to change, but if the crisis does not drag on for too long, we could still have three percent growth," he said.
Walter Molano, of SBC Warburg, was a tad more optimistic. "Inflation could be more or less the same as last year, a bit above 21 percent," he said by telephone from New York.
Inflation closed 1996 at 25.5 percent and GDP grew 1.8 percent.
On growth, Molano predicted 1.5 to 2.0 percent "with investors freezing everything until the situation clears up."
Local analyst Fidel Jaramillo -- who forecasts inflation to reach up to 38 percent in 1997 -- said the main worry of the transitional administration is likely to be fiscal.

Any reversal of the harsh economic measures that Bucaram planned to take but had already rolled back -- including steep public sector rate increases and subsidy cuts -- are likely to widen the fiscal deficit from a projected 2.5 percent of GDP.
"This will undoubtedly be the major headache" of the next government, he said.
